newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa killings could sink shaky KwaZulu truce.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa killings could sink shaky KwaZulu truce.

text.p: Violence returned to South Africa's troubled KwaZulu-Natal province over the Christmas holiday period, with 31 people shot dead in six massacres since early December.

Gangs of killers with automatic weapons stalked the mainly rural Zulu heartland, sometimes wiping out whole families in feuds -- most political, some over resources, some over distant disagreements from generations ago.
The renewed killing undermines a truce brokered by President Nelson Mandela and holds a knife to the throat of investment in this naturally rich territory.

"These killings come at the end of a year where there was a lot of positiveness. It is distressing because it could impact immediately and negatively on investment in KwaZulu-Natal," said Durban Chamber of Commerce and Industry president Rob Stretch.
"Over the past 18 months we have had quite a lot of investment. But investors could look to other provinces if the violence does increase again."

The latest spate of late-night attacks on lonely homesteads by men armed with the ubiquitous AK-47 assault rifle can be linked to workers returning to their farms from cities for the Christmas break and organising attacks, said a peace worker.
"People coming from the cities sometimes take the law into their own hands because policing and justice in the rural areas is so poor," peace committee chairman Mthokozisi Ngubane said.
"They also feed into the political tensions in the area," he told Reuters, adding that easy access to firearms and a culture of violence was exacerbating the situation.

The massacres are an indication that a fragile six-month-old peace agreement between two major political parties in KwaZulu-Natal was in serious trouble, said Network of Independent Monitors spokeswoman Jenni Irish.
"There has been a rise in (political) tensions over the past three months and it culminated in the killings around Christmas...it is definitely jeopardising the peace process."

Monitors said Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC) and their fiercest black political rivals, the Inkatha Freedom Party, are still locked in a struggle to dominate KwaZulu-Natal, home to nine million Zulus.

In addition to the 31 who died in bloody raids, a further 10 were killed in single politically motivated attacks in December, bringing to 454 the death toll for 1996, compared to 837 for 1995, the independent Human Rights Committee (HRC) said.

"The peace process has largely been between political leaders and has not filtered down to the communities which, until they believe in it and make it work, will continue to be plagued by violence," said HRC researcher Makubetse Sekhonyane.
The peace accord took effect in June 1996, weeks before a local government election which Inkatha, the ruling party in the province, won despite ANC victories in the major cities.
The ANC has proposed a peace package which would give Kwazulu-Natal a special amnesty provision.

However, Inkatha leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi this week rejected the amnesty deal, saying "there was a war going on full swing" and an amnesty process would merely sweep the truth "under a carpet of silence and lies".
"We cannot accept that those who died did so in vain, and that those who blindly killed or orchestrated the violence from high-ranking political positions may elude responsibility."

Inkatha has not endorsed South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which is probing 30 years of apartheid-era atrocities and has the authority to grant amnesty, saying the process is biased in favour of the ANC.
It also boycotted the writing of a new constitution.
Chamber of Commerce chief Stretch said Buthelezi's position was causing alarm.

"This continued standoff cannot go on. It seems that at provincial level there are serious attempts by the parties to cooperate...Buthelezi has got to be very careful about what he says about the process," he said.
